  [inst : NormedAddCommGroup E] →

fun E [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] [MeasurableSpace E] =>
  MeasureTheory.Measure.map (fun x => ∑ i, x i • (stdOrthonormalBasis ℝ E) i)
    (MeasureTheory.Measure.pi fun x => ProbabilityTheory.gaussianReal 0 1)
def ProbabilityTheory.gaussianReal : ℝ → NNReal → MeasureTheory.Measure ℝ :=
fun μ v =>
  if v = 0 then MeasureTheory.Measure.dirac μ else MeasureTheory.volume.withDensity (ProbabilityTheory.gaussianPDF μ v)
def ProbabilityTheory.gaussianPDF : ℝ → NNReal → ℝ → ENNReal :=
fun μ v x => ENNReal.ofReal (ProbabilityTheory.gaussianPDFReal μ v x)
def ProbabilityTheory.gaussianPDFReal : ℝ → NNReal → ℝ → ℝ :=
fun μ v x => (√(2 * Real.pi * ↑v))⁻¹ * Real.exp (-(x - μ) ^ 2 / (2 * ↑v))

reconstruction.text:
Let E be an arbitrary finite-dimensional real inner-product space with its compatible norm and Borel measurable structure. Write gamma_E for the measure defined by stdGaussian E. Concretely, if (e_k) is the standard orthonormal basis used in the definition, gamma_E is the pushforward of the finite product of real Gaussian laws gaussianReal(0,1) by (z_k) -> sum_k z_k e_k. The supplied density fixes each coordinate law as (2*pi)^(-1/2) exp(-t^2/2) dt: the mean is zero and the variance is one. Thus the Gaussian normalization is specified, not an unspecified scale. All integrals below are real Bochner/Lebesgue integrals over the whole E with respect to this same gamma_E.

Let u and v be any vectors in E with ||u||=1 and ||v||=1, and let i,j be arbitrary natural numbers, including zero. Define polynomials H_m in Z[X] by the supplied recurrence
 H_0(X)=1,
 H_(m+1)(X)=X H_m(X)-H_m'(X).
In real-valued formulas H_m(t) means evaluation at t after mapping each integer coefficient into R. This is exactly Polynomial.aeval t (Polynomial.hermite m). The recurrence gives H_1(t)=t and H_2(t)=t^2-1 and fixes the normalization; no factorial or square-root-factorial normalization is applied to H_m itself.

Define the actual real function on E
 G(x)=H_i(<u,x>) H_j(<v,x>).
Then G is integrable with respect to gamma_E and
 integral_E G(x) d gamma_E(x)
   = { i! * <u,v>^i, if i=j;
       0,             if i!=j. }

The factorial i! is a natural number cast to R, and the power is the ordinary real base <u,v> raised to the natural exponent i. It is not |<u,v>|^i, so the sign for negative overlap and odd i is retained. The zero-degree case uses 0!=1 and a^0=1, including a=0. The measure is the same standard Gaussian for both factors, so this is a shared-x mixed moment; no independence, orthogonality, or linear independence of u and v is assumed. The only vector restrictions are their two unit-norm conditions. There is no additional lower bound on dim E, although in dimension zero unit vectors do not exist. Integrability of G is part of the conclusion rather than a premise. The theorem does not separately assert that either factor belongs to L2, an orthonormal-basis completeness result, or a joint-law construction. There is no time parameter, horizon, limiting sense or existential constant.
